title: Detection Strategy for T1505.002 - Transport Agent Abuse (Windows/Linux)
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for T1505.002 - Transport Agent Abuse ...
summary: This strategy detects abuse of mail transport agents, the components that accept, route and deliver email, where an attacker adds or alters an agent or transport rule so that messages are copied, redirected or injected without the users or administrators noticing. The covered technique matters because the mail server is a trusted relay with access to internal and external conversations, so a hidden agent provides persistent collection and a quiet outbound channel that blends with ordinary mail. File integrity monitoring of mail configuration, mail server logs and process execution records make it possible, because a new agent or transport rule requires a file change and leaves a distinct process and message flow. The main failure mode is that administrators change mail configuration for legitimate reasons and mail servers are extremely chatty, so the rule must anchor on the modification plus the resulting anomalous flow rather than on message volume.

beginner.definition: This detection watches the parts of a mail server that decide where email goes. An attacker can add a hidden rule or program that copies messages elsewhere. The mail keeps flowing normally, so nobody complains.
beginner.whyItMatters: A mail server already has permission to read and send mail, so an added rule inherits that trust. It can quietly copy every message to an outside address, which is a serious data loss. A hidden agent can also be used to send messages that look internal. Configuration changes are rare and reviewable, which makes detection practical.
howItWorks: The mail server keeps its routing logic in configuration files and agent programs.
A file monitoring tool records whenever those files or programs change.
The mail log records each message, its sender, its recipients and the route taken.
The detection links the configuration change to the messages that follow it.
It looks for new recipients outside the organisation or unusual forwarding patterns.
An analyst confirms whether a change ticket explains both the change and the flow.
beginner.example: Think of a company post room where staff sort all incoming letters. Someone adds a standing instruction that every letter from the finance desk is also photocopied to an outside address. The post room keeps working normally, and only the instruction sheet shows what changed.
takeaways: Monitor mail configuration and agent directories as security critical, not routine.
Link a configuration change to the message flows that appear afterwards.
Watch for outside recipients and forwarding patterns that the business does not expect.

objectives: Describe what a mail transport agent does and why adding one is a persistence technique.
Identify the configuration paths and agent directories that must be integrity monitored.
Read mail log entries to reconstruct the route and recipients of a suspicious message.
Correlate a configuration change with new outside recipients or unexpected forwarding.
Explain how an added agent can both collect mail and provide an outbound channel.
dataSources: File integrity monitoring alerts for mail server configuration files, transport rule stores, agent and plugin directories, and message routing tables
Mail server logs recording message identifier, sender, recipients, queue identifier, transport used and delivery status
Linux auditd execve records for mail transport and queue management binaries such as sendmail, postfix and their helper programs
Configuration management or change records for the mail platform showing approved edits and the administrator who applied them
logic: The pattern is a change to the components that decide message routing, followed by message flows that the organisation cannot explain. The telemetry is the file integrity alert on mail configuration and agent paths, the mail server log entries for messages, the auditd execution records for mail binaries, and the change management record, and the fields that must be correlated are the file path and hash that changed, the account and process that changed it, the message identifiers and recipient addresses that follow, the transport or route selected, and the time gap between the change and the new flow. Benign behaviour is a documented change to a relay host or a spam filter plugin applied from the mail administrator's session, with delivery patterns that continue to match the previous baseline. Malicious behaviour is a new transport rule or agent binary appearing outside a maintenance window, created by an account that does not normally manage mail, followed within minutes by messages leaving to external addresses the organisation does not know, or by a steady stream of copies of internal mail toward a single outside destination. The pairing of the file change with the new flow is essential, because either signal alone is common on a busy mail server and together they describe a hidden copy rule.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Mail transport configuration changed followed by new external recipients
# logsource:
#   product: linux
#   service: fileintegrity
# detection:
#   selection_change:
#     file|startswith:
#       - '/etc/postfix/'
#       - '/etc/mail/'
#       - '/usr/libexec/postfix/'
#     action:
#       - created
#       - modified
#   filter_mailadmins:
#     user:
#       - 'mailadmin'
#       - 'cmdb-agent'
#   condition: selection_change and not filter_mailadmins
# level: high
falsePositives: Mail administrators applying an approved relay or transport map change during a maintenance window
Configuration management tooling that rewrites mail configuration files to enforce the declared state on every run
Package upgrades that replace mail binaries and plugin libraries, producing many file changes at once
A legitimate migration between mail platforms where routing is adjusted over several days
Antispam or data loss prevention plugins that install or update their own transport hooks on a schedule
tuningNotes: Build the baseline from the configuration management system rather than from observed file changes, so that expected rewrites by automation are excluded by process and signer, and keep interactive edits by humans alertable. Scope the file watch to the transport, agent and plugin paths only, because watching the entire mail directory produces constant noise from queue and cache files. Set a correlation window of fifteen to thirty minutes between the change and the new recipient pattern using your own message volume baseline. The coverage you lose by excluding configuration management is abuse performed through that same tool, so monitor its credentials separately and alert on any mail configuration change it makes outside a scheduled deployment. Also alert on new external recipient domains seen for the first time, because that signal survives even when the file change is missed.
